entries.title: Global disclosure regime map
facts: EU: CSRD/ESRS applies double materiality with phased scope from FY2024 (large public-interest entities), though the 2025 Omnibus package reduced scope and delayed later waves.
US: the SEC climate rule (adopted March 2024) was stayed pending litigation and later withdrawn from defence; California SB 253/261 press ahead for large companies doing business there.
30+ jurisdictions are adopting ISSB standards, including Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, Brazil, UK (endorsement route), Japan and Hong Kong.

entries.title: EU CBAM essentials
facts: CBAM covers iron & steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen; transitional reporting ran from October 2023, with financial obligations (certificate purchase) from 2026.
Exporters to the EU must report embedded emissions per product using EU methodology — a direct commercial driver for GHG accounting in every exporting steel and aluminium producer.

entries.title: Case study — Interface Mission Zero
facts: Interface (carpet tiles) ran Mission Zero (1994–2019), cutting manufacturing GHG intensity ~96% and proving industrial decarbonisation pays back through material efficiency and recycled inputs.
Its successor programme, Climate Take Back, targets carbon-negative products — carbon-storing tiles reached market in 2020.

entries.title: Case study — IKEA value-chain programme
facts: IKEA targets halving absolute value-chain emissions by 2030 (vs FY2016) while growing — its footprint is >95% Scope 3, driving supplier renewable-energy financing programmes.
Pattern to reuse: when Scope 3 dominates, capital support for supplier decarbonisation beats reporting requests alone.

entries.title: Internal carbon pricing practice
facts: Two models: shadow price (stress-tests capex decisions; typical US$40–150/t) and internal fee (charges business units real money — Microsoft's fee funds its removals portfolio).
CDP data shows >2,000 companies using or planning internal carbon pricing; effectiveness depends on the price actually binding in investment decisions.

entries.title: SBTi validation process
facts: Route: commit (letter) → develop targets within 24 months → submit for validation (fee-based, booked via SBTi portal) → announce within 6 months of approval → disclose progress annually.
Common rejection causes: base-year emissions coverage below 95% of Scope 1+2, missing Scope 3 target when ≥40% of footprint, and intensity targets where absolute is required.

entries.title: Renewable procurement instruments
facts: Hierarchy of credibility: on-site generation > physical PPA > virtual PPA > bundled RECs/green tariffs > unbundled RECs (RE100 accepts all but market rules apply).
24/7 carbon-free energy matching (hourly, not annual) is the emerging leadership bar, pioneered by Google's 2030 commitment.
Routes vary by market: corporate PPAs and guarantees of origin dominate in Europe, while other markets rely on green tariffs and tradable certificates on power exchanges.

entries.title: Report gap-analysis method
facts: A rigorous gap analysis maps each disclosure to specific framework paragraphs (e.g. IFRS S2 para 29(a) for Scope 3), classifies coverage as full/partial/absent, and ranks gaps by regulatory exposure and investor salience.
Quick wins usually found: missing methodology notes (GWP set, factor vintages), no base-year recalculation policy, and targets stated without interim milestones.

entries.title: ISSA 5000 — the new umbrella standard
facts: ISSA 5000 (approved by IAASB September 2024) is the comprehensive standard for sustainability assurance, applying to any framework (ISSB, GRI, ESRS) and both limited and reasonable assurance.
It is effective for periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026, replacing reliance on ISAE 3000/3410 for sustainability engagements.
It is profession-agnostic — usable by audit firms and other assurance practitioners.

entries.title: Limited vs reasonable assurance
facts: Limited assurance: negative-form conclusion ('nothing came to our attention'), evidence mainly inquiry + analytical procedures; cost and effort materially lower.
Reasonable assurance: positive opinion ('fairly stated'), audit-equivalent evidence — walkthroughs, controls testing, substantive detail testing, recalculation.
Most regimes phase limited → reasonable (Australia reaches reasonable assurance for climate disclosures for FYs from 1 July 2030).

entries.title: Materiality in GHG assurance
facts: Practitioners commonly set planning materiality around 5% of total reported emissions (the relevant base), with performance materiality at 50–75% of that as a buffer.
Clearly trivial threshold is typically ~5% of planning materiality — misstatements below it aren't accumulated.
Qualitative materiality matters too: a small misstatement that flips a stated target from 'met' to 'missed' is material regardless of size.

entries.title: Evidence pack (PBC) expectations
facts: Standard PBC list: boundary memo + entity list, methodology note (factors, GWP set, estimates), activity-data extracts with source-system screenshots, factor library with vintages, certificates (RECs/PPAs), base-year recalculation policy, and sign-off trail.
Practitioners sample high-value lines first: electricity invoices vs kWh claimed, fuel purchase records vs litres, and Scope 3 category-15 attribution workings for FIs.

entries.title: Australia assurance phasing (AUASB)
facts: AUASB's phased approach: year-one assurance covers governance disclosures and Scope 1–2 (limited), expanding across all climate disclosures, reaching reasonable assurance for FYs commencing from 1 July 2030.
The auditor of the financial report is expected to conduct the sustainability assurance for consistency of materiality and group scoping.

entries.title: Top recurring assurance findings
facts: Most common findings across GHG engagements: outdated emission factors, incomplete entity/facility coverage, unit conversion errors (GJ/MWh/kWh), estimation presented as measurement, market-based Scope 2 without valid certificates, and Scope 3 category omissions without justification.
Remediating before fieldwork is far cheaper than post-finding restatement — a readiness scan against these six items is standard practice.

entries.title: Typical engagement timeline
facts: A first-year limited-assurance engagement typically runs 14–18 weeks: scoping & independence (2), planning & risk assessment (3), interim walkthroughs (3), fieldwork (4–6), review, findings and reporting (3).
Booking the practitioner before year-end close and agreeing the PBC list early are the two biggest schedule savers.

entries.title: NGFS scenario families
facts: NGFS scenarios group into Orderly (Net Zero 2050, Below 2°C), Disorderly (Delayed Transition), Hot House World (Current Policies, NDCs), and Too-Little-Too-Late (Fragmented World).
Net Zero 2050 assumes immediate coordinated policy, ~1.4–1.5°C in 2100, high transition risk but low physical risk; Current Policies reaches ~3°C with severe physical risk.
NGFS Phase V (Nov 2024) updated damage functions — chronic physical damages materially higher than earlier phases.

entries.title: Carbon price trajectories by scenario
facts: In NGFS Net Zero 2050, modelled global carbon prices reach roughly US$100–200/tCO2 by 2030 and several hundred by 2050 (model-dependent).
Delayed Transition scenarios show low prices this decade then a sharp spike after 2030 — the signature 'disorderly' shock to test in stress scenarios.
Use scenario carbon prices as shadow prices on Scope 1+2 to estimate EBITDA-at-risk.

entries.title: Physical risk hazard set (IPCC AR6)
facts: Acute hazards: riverine/coastal flood, tropical cyclone, heatwave, wildfire, drought; chronic: sea-level rise, water stress, mean temperature rise, precipitation shift.
AR6 projects sea-level rise of ~0.28–0.55 m by 2100 under low emissions and ~0.63–1.01 m under very high emissions.
South Asia is a flagged hotspot for compounding heat-humidity risk; wet-bulb thresholds constrain outdoor labour productivity.

entries.title: TCFD scenario analysis expectations
facts: TCFD (and IFRS S2 para 22) expect scenario analysis proportional to the entity's exposure, including at least one ≤2°C scenario, with disclosure of assumptions, time horizons and resilience conclusions.
Good practice pairs one orderly, one disorderly and one hot-house scenario, and quantifies impact on revenue, costs, and asset values by segment.

entries.title: APRA CPS 229 climate risk expectations
facts: APRA's prudential guidance (CPG 229) expects regulated entities to embed climate risk in governance, risk appetite and scenario analysis; the Climate Vulnerability Assessment ran with the five largest banks.
AASB S2 reporting and APRA expectations interlock: scenario analysis capabilities built for CVA feed directly into mandatory disclosure.

entries.title: Case study — Ørsted's transition
facts: Ørsted transformed from ~85% fossil-based heat & power (as DONG Energy) to ~90% renewable generation within a decade, divesting upstream oil & gas in 2017.
It is the textbook example of pre-empting stranded-asset risk by redirecting capex — cited in most transition-planning guidance.

entries.title: GFANZ transition plan framework
facts: GFANZ recommends transition plans across five themes: foundations, implementation strategy, engagement strategy, metrics & targets, and governance.
Credible plans distinguish financing emissions reduction ('financed reductions') from portfolio decarbonisation via divestment, which shifts rather than cuts real-economy emissions.

entries.title: TNFD and nature-related risk
facts: TNFD's final recommendations (Sept 2023) mirror TCFD's four pillars and add the LEAP process: Locate interface with nature, Evaluate dependencies/impacts, Assess risks/opportunities, Prepare to respond.
Priority sectors: agriculture, food, mining, energy, infrastructure and financial institutions exposed to them.

entries.title: Case study — CBA climate scenario disclosure
facts: Commonwealth Bank's annual climate report discloses sector-level financed-emissions baselines and glidepaths, plus physical-risk maps of its mortgage book by postcode-level hazard exposure.
Mortgage-book flood/cyclone exposure analysis is the leading example of translating physical hazards into credit metrics for AASB S2.

entries.title: MAS environmental risk management (Singapore)
facts: MAS ERM Guidelines (2020) require banks, insurers and asset managers to embed environmental risk in governance, risk management and disclosure, with board-level accountability.
MAS industry stress tests have included long-run climate scenarios aligned to NGFS pathways; disclosure expectations reference TCFD/ISSB alignment.

entries.title: Credit quality fundamentals
facts: A high-quality credit demonstrates additionality (wouldn't happen without credit revenue), permanence (reversal risk managed via buffer pools), no leakage (emissions don't shift elsewhere), and robust MRV.
ICVCM's Core Carbon Principles (2023) are the leading quality benchmark; CCP-labelled methodologies signal integrity to buyers.
Avoidance/reduction credits (e.g. REDD+, cookstoves) trade at a discount to durable removals (DAC, biochar, mineralisation).

entries.title: Registries and standards
facts: Verra's VCS is the largest voluntary registry by issuance; Gold Standard emphasises SDG co-benefits; others include ACR, CAR and Puro.earth (removals).
Every credit carries: registry ID, methodology, vintage year, project location, and verification body — retirement is recorded publicly on the registry.
Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement is creating a UN-supervised international crediting mechanism alongside voluntary markets.

entries.title: Blue carbon science
facts: Mangroves, seagrasses and tidal marshes sequester carbon per hectare at multiples of tropical forests, largely in sediment that stays stored for centuries if undisturbed.
Mangroves also deliver storm-surge protection and fisheries co-benefits, supporting premium pricing; Verra VM0033 is the main tidal-wetland methodology.
Mangrove and seagrass coastlines across Southeast Asia, East Africa and Latin America host the bulk of restorable blue-carbon potential.

entries.title: Using credits in net-zero claims
facts: SBTi's Net-Zero Standard restricts credits to neutralising residual emissions (≤5–10%) at net-zero, not substituting for near-term abatement; interim use is 'beyond value chain mitigation'.
The mitigation hierarchy: reduce first, then remove, then offset — regulators (ACCC, CMA) have pursued greenwashing claims built on low-quality offsets.
IFRS S2 para 36(e) requires disclosing planned carbon-credit use: volume, type (reduction vs removal), registry and quality assumptions.

entries.title: Case study — Microsoft removals portfolio
facts: Microsoft (carbon negative by 2030 pledge, 2020) runs the largest corporate durable-removals procurement programme — multi-year offtakes across DAC, BECCS, biochar and mineralisation, published in an annual sustainability report with contracted volumes.
Its RFP criteria (durability >100 years, additionality, verifiability) have become de-facto buyer standards for removals.

entries.title: Plastic credits landscape
facts: Plastic credits (1 credit = 1 kg or 1 tonne collected/recycled, standard-dependent) run on Verra's Plastic Waste Reduction Program, PCX, and certifiers like CleanHub and rePurpose Global.
Quality hinges on chain-of-custody evidence and additionality versus existing municipal collection; social co-benefits (waste-picker formalisation) drive premiums.
Plastic credits are not carbon credits — they cannot support climate claims, only plastic-footprint claims.

entries.title: Biodiversity credits (emerging)
facts: Biodiversity credit schemes (e.g. Terrasos habitat units in Colombia, Australia's Nature Repair Market from 2025) quantify ecosystem uplift per unit area and time.
Unlike carbon, there is no fungible global unit — buyers should treat biodiversity units as project-specific contributions, not offsets against harm.
Measurement typically combines species richness, habitat condition and threat-reduction indices, increasingly verified with eDNA and remote sensing.

entries.title: Tokenised credits — cautions
facts: Tokenisation puts registry credits on-chain for fractional trade and transparent retirement, but registries (Verra 2022) banned tokenising retired credits after bridge schemes created zombie-credit risk.
Credible tokenised markets require live two-way registry bridges so on-chain retirement burns the underlying registry credit exactly once.

entries.title: Price benchmarks by category
facts: Indicative voluntary-market ranges (2024–25): nature avoidance (REDD+) ~US$3–10/t, cookstoves ~US$5–15/t, ARR reforestation ~US$15–40/t, blue carbon premium ~US$20–40/t, durable removals US$100–600+/t.
Prices vary sharply with vintage, rating-agency scores (BeZero, Sylvera) and co-benefits — always quote a range, never a point price.

entries.title: PRI due diligence framing
facts: The PRI's LP responsible-investment DDQ structures GP assessment around policy & governance, ESG integration in investment process, portfolio monitoring, and reporting to LPs.
ILPA's ESG assessment framework grades GP maturity from 'not yet started' to 'leading' across the same dimensions — useful for scoring rubrics.

entries.title: SFDR fund classifications
facts: SFDR Article 6 = no sustainability claim; Article 8 = promotes E/S characteristics; Article 9 = sustainable investment objective with do-no-significant-harm and PAI reporting.
Article 9 funds must hold ~100% 'sustainable investments' (per ESMA clarifications), which drove a wave of 2022–23 downgrades to Article 8.

entries.title: ICMA Green Bond Principles
facts: GBP's four pillars: use of proceeds, process for project evaluation & selection, management of proceeds, and reporting (allocation + impact).
A Second Party Opinion (SPO) assesses alignment pre-issuance; leading providers include Sustainalytics, S&P Global (Shades of Green), Moody's and ISS.
Impact reporting typically quantifies tCO2e avoided, renewable capacity added, or equivalent metrics per the Harmonised Framework.

entries.title: ESG-credit risk linkage (banking)
facts: Basel Committee principles (2022) expect banks to embed climate risk in credit assessment: borrower transition plans, collateral physical exposure, and sector heatmaps feeding PD/LGD adjustments.
Common practice: an ESG score notch adjustment to internal ratings, capped so it can't override fundamental credit deterioration.

entries.title: Supplier engagement (CDP Supply Chain pattern)
facts: Effective supplier programmes tier by spend and emissions: top ~20 suppliers usually cover 60–80% of category-1 emissions — start disclosure requests there.
Escalation ladder: information request → improvement plan → contractual clauses → procurement preference/exclusion; CDP Supply Chain membership operationalises the request step.
Ask for supplier-specific (not industry-average) emission factors as maturity grows — it converts spend-based estimates into activity-based data.

entries.title: Case study — engagement beats exclusion
facts: Climate Action 100+ (700+ investors, ~US$68tn AUM at peak) demonstrated coordinated engagement outcomes: majority of focus companies set net-zero ambitions during its first phase.
DD implication: assess a GP/bank's stewardship evidence (voting records, escalation outcomes), not just exclusion lists.

entries.title: Greenwashing enforcement precedents
facts: ASIC's first greenwashing court outcomes (2024) — including against Mercer and Vanguard — established that unsubstantiated ESG screens/claims in fund marketing attract civil penalties.
DD checklists should verify that every public ESG claim maps to a documented, auditable process.

entries.title: CSRD scope after the Omnibus
facts: An EU company is in scope only if it exceeds BOTH 1,000 employees AND EUR 450mn net turnover — the Omnibus made this an AND test, taking a large number of previously in-scope companies out.
Non-EU parent groups are tested instead on EU-generated turnover above EUR 450mn.
Wave 1 companies continue reporting; Wave 2 first reports are due in 2028 covering FY2027, deferred by the Omnibus from the original timetable.

entries.title: The revised ESRS adopted July 2026
facts: The European Commission adopted the delegated act containing the revised, simplified ESRS on 3 July 2026, cutting mandatory datapoints by 61% against the 2023 standards.

The revised standards apply to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Reports being prepared now for FY2025 and FY2026 are still filed against ESRS Set 1, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772.
A scrutiny period of two months with the Parliament and Council, extendable by two more, runs before entry into force — so the commencement date is not yet certain.

entries.title: Double materiality against financial materiality
facts: ESRS requires a topic to be reported if it is material to people and the environment OR material to the company. IFRS S2 requires only the second.
An IFRS S2 or AASB S2 materiality assessment is therefore never sufficient evidence for omitting an ESRS topical standard — the impact side has to be assessed separately.
Every omitted topical standard needs a stated reason, and omitting ESRS E1 attracts an explicit explanation requirement.

entries.title: EU Taxonomy Article 8 KPIs
facts: Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 requires disclosure of the proportion of turnover, CapEx and OpEx associated with Taxonomy-aligned activities — three separate KPIs, each a ratio over its own defined denominator.

Alignment requires four things: the activity is eligible, it substantially contributes to one of the six environmental objectives, it does no significant harm to the other five, and the entity meets minimum safeguards.

Minimum safeguards are assessed at entity level against the OECD Guidelines and the UN Guiding Principles, so failing them zeroes alignment across all three KPIs rather than dropping a single activity.
Credit institutions report the Green Asset Ratio instead; the turnover, CapEx and OpEx KPIs are treated as less relevant for financial undertakings.

entries.title: EU Taxonomy reporting simplification 2026
facts: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/73 was published in the Official Journal on 8 January 2026 and entered into force on 28 January 2026, applying from 1 January 2026.

Activities representing less than 10% of turnover, CapEx or OpEx need not be assessed, and the test is applied to each KPI independently — so the same activity can be excluded from one KPI and assessed in another.
A company may omit the OpEx KPI entirely where it is not material to its business model, disclosing only the total value and why it is not material.
Reporting templates were cut by roughly 64% of datapoints for non-financial undertakings and 89% for financial institutions, consolidated into one summary table and up to three per-activity tables.

entries.title: XBRL tagging of the sustainability statement
facts: Mandatory XBRL tagging of the CSRD sustainability statement is suspended by Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force 18 March 2026, until the ESEF Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/815 is amended to cover sustainability tagging.

The ESRS Set 1 XBRL taxonomy itself exists and is published by EFRAG, covering over 1,200 datapoints; EFRAG is committed to delivering an updated taxonomy against the revised standards by December 2026.
Resumption depends on ESMA drafting regulatory technical standards and the Commission amending the ESEF regulation — neither has happened, so no firm resumption date exists.

entries.title: What carries across from IFRS S2 to ESRS
facts: The IFRS Foundation and EFRAG published joint Interoperability Guidance on 2 May 2024, mapping the climate requirements of IFRS S2 against ESRS 1, ESRS 2 and ESRS E1.

The strongest carry-across is the GHG inventory: both require gross Scope 1, 2 and 3 measured under the GHG Protocol, with Scope 2 on both location and market basis, so an inventory built for one serves the other.

ESRS asks for more on transition plans, on targets consistent with a 1.5°C pathway, and on the operating and capital expenditure attached to climate actions. IFRS S2 asks for industry-based metrics referencing SASB, which ESRS Set 1 has no equivalent for.

entries.title: The value chain cap
facts: A CSRD reporter may not require a company in its value chain with 1,000 employees or fewer to provide more sustainability information than the voluntary standard requires.

Gross Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions are carved out of that cap, so the emissions ask survives it — which is why an SME supplier still needs an inventory even when the rest of the questionnaire is capped.

entries.title: GHG Protocol scopes and boundaries
facts: Scope 1 = direct emissions from owned/controlled sources; Scope 2 = purchased energy; Scope 3 = all other value-chain emissions across 15 defined categories.
Organisational boundary uses either equity share or control (financial or operational) — the choice must be documented and applied consistently.
Scope 2 dual reporting: both location-based (grid average) and market-based (contractual instruments) figures are required by the Scope 2 Guidance.

entries.title: The 15 Scope 3 categories
facts: Upstream: 1 purchased goods & services, 2 capital goods, 3 fuel & energy related, 4 upstream transport, 5 waste, 6 business travel, 7 commuting, 8 upstream leased assets.
Downstream: 9 downstream transport, 10 processing of sold products, 11 use of sold products, 12 end-of-life, 13 downstream leased assets, 14 franchises, 15 investments (financed emissions).
For most financial institutions, category 15 dominates — often >95% of total footprint.

entries.title: PCAF financed emissions methodology
facts: PCAF attribution: financed emissions = (outstanding amount ÷ EVIC or total equity+debt) × borrower/investee emissions.
Data quality scores run 1 (audited, reported emissions) to 5 (economic-activity proxies); portfolios disclose an exposure-weighted average score.
PCAF Standard v2 (2022) covers seven asset classes including listed equity, business loans, project finance, mortgages, commercial real estate and sovereign debt.

entries.title: GWP values (IPCC AR6, 100-year)
facts: Common refrigerants: R-410A ≈ 2,088, R-134a ≈ 1,430, R-32 ≈ 675, R-404A ≈ 3,922 — a small leak of R-404A outweighs tonnes of CO2.
IFRS S2 and most regulators now expect AR5 or AR6 GWP sets, stated explicitly in the methodology note.

entries.title: Common emission factors (DEFRA 2024)
facts: Diesel ≈ 2.68 kgCO2e/litre; petrol ≈ 2.31 kgCO2e/litre; natural gas ≈ 56.1 kgCO2e/GJ (≈2.04 kg/m³).
Average economy long-haul flight ≈ 0.15–0.20 kgCO2e per passenger-km including radiative forcing; UK DEFRA publishes updated factors every June.
Landfilled mixed municipal waste ≈ 0.45–0.6 tCO2e per tonne depending on composition.

entries.title: SBTi reduction pathways
facts: SBTi's cross-sector 1.5°C pathway requires a minimum 4.2% absolute reduction per year for Scope 1+2 near-term targets.
Scope 3 targets are required when Scope 3 is ≥40% of total emissions; near-term Scope 3 ambition minimum is well-below-2°C (≈2.5%/yr).
The Net-Zero Standard requires 90–95% absolute reduction by 2050 with residual emissions neutralised by permanent removals.

entries.title: Verification and audit-trail expectations
facts: Verifiers (ISAE 3410 / ISSA 5000) trace each inventory line to: activity data source, emission factor + vintage, calculation, and responsible owner.
Classic findings: stale emission factors (3+ years old), unit errors (GJ vs MWh), market-based claims without retired certificates, and double counting across scopes.
Keep a base-year recalculation policy — structural changes (M&A, divestment, methodology) above a threshold (commonly 5%) trigger restatement.

entries.title: Case study — Infosys carbon neutrality
facts: Infosys declared carbon neutrality from FY2020 (PAS 2060), combining on-site solar, RE procurement and community-based offset projects covering Scope 1–3.
Its published ESG data book itemises emissions by scope and category with third-party assurance — a strong reference for IT-services inventories.

entries.title: IFRS S2 core structure
facts: IFRS S2 requires disclosure across four TCFD-aligned pillars: Governance (paras 5–9), Strategy (paras 8–23), Risk Management (paras 24–26), Metrics & Targets (paras 27–37).
Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions are mandatory under para 29(a), measured per the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard unless a jurisdiction requires otherwise.
Scope 2 must be reported location-based, with market-based information disclosed where contractual instruments exist.

entries.title: IFRS S2 transition reliefs
facts: First-year reliefs: entities may omit Scope 3 emissions, comparatives, and may report sustainability disclosures with second-quarter interim reporting rather than with the annual report.
The Scope 3 relief lasts one annual reporting period; after that, Scope 3 measurement per the GHG Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard is required.

entries.title: AASB S2 Australian phase-in groups
facts: Group 1 (two of: revenue ≥ A$500m, assets ≥ A$1bn, employees ≥ 500) reports for financial years starting 1 January 2025.
Group 2 (two of: A$200m revenue, A$500m assets, 250 employees) starts FYs from 1 July 2026; Group 3 (A$50m revenue, A$25m assets, 100 employees) from 1 July 2027.
Scope 3, scenario analysis and transition plan statements have a 3-year 'protected statements' regime — only ASIC can take action in that window.

entries.title: Singapore SGX climate reporting timeline
facts: SGX-listed issuers move to mandatory ISSB-aligned climate reporting from FY2025, starting with larger issuers; large non-listed companies (revenue ≥ S$1bn) follow from FY2027.
Reporting was previously phased comply-or-explain from FY2022 under SGX's sustainability reporting regime, with mandatory climate reporting for finance, agri-food and energy sectors from FY2023.

entries.title: GRI–ISSB interoperability
facts: ISSB standards use investor-focused (single) materiality; GRI uses impact materiality — companies commonly report both, and the GRI–IFRS Foundation interoperability work maps GRI 305 emissions disclosures to IFRS S2 requirements.
GRI 305 (Emissions) categories align with GHG Protocol scopes, so one inventory can feed both a GRI report and an IFRS S2 disclosure.

entries.title: Case study — DBS climate disclosure practice
facts: DBS has published TCFD-aligned disclosures since 2018 and detailed sector-level financed-emissions targets in its 'Our Path to Net Zero' report (2022), covering nine sectors including power, oil & gas, and real estate.
Its approach — sector glidepaths benchmarked to IEA NZE — is a widely cited template for bank ISSB S2 metrics & targets sections.

entries.title: Materiality assessment good practice
facts: A defensible materiality process documents: stakeholder groups consulted, scoring criteria, threshold for 'material', board sign-off, and refresh cadence (typically annual or biennial).
Under IFRS S1/S2, information is material if omitting it could influence investor decisions — impact-only topics belong in GRI/CSRD-style reports instead.

entries.title: CDP alignment with ISSB
facts: CDP's climate questionnaire incorporated IFRS S2 from the 2024 cycle, so an IFRS S2-ready disclosure substantially pre-fills CDP responses.
CDP scores A to D-; an A requires leadership-level disclosure including verified emissions and robust scenario-informed transition planning.

entries.title: GHG Protocol organisational boundary choices
facts: Three consolidation approaches: equity share (emissions by share of equity, reflecting economic interest), financial control (100% of emissions where the company has financial control) and operational control (100% where it has authority to introduce and implement operating policies).
The choice must be disclosed, not merely made, and applied consistently. Changing it is a structural change that triggers base year recalculation.

Under a control approach a company accounts for none of the emissions of operations it holds an interest in but does not control — which is why two companies can report very different totals for the same joint venture.

entries.title: What a GHG Protocol report must disclose
facts: A reporting company must disclose its organisational boundary including the consolidation approach, its operational boundary including the activity types covered where Scope 3 is reported, and its base year with the recalculation policy and significance threshold.
Gross emissions for the chosen inventory boundary must be presented separately from and independently of any GHG trades or offsets.

Scope 1 and Scope 2 are the minimum. Scope 3 is optional under the Corporate Standard itself — the reason companies report it is usually IFRS S2 paragraph 29(a), ESRS E1-6 or a customer's value chain request, not the Corporate Standard.
The Scope 2 Guidance requires dual reporting: a location-based figure using average grid factors and a market-based figure reflecting contractual instruments. Neither replaces the other.

entries.title: ISO 14064-1:2018 six categories
facts: ISO 14064-1:2018 replaced the three-scope model with six categories: 1 direct emissions and removals, 2 imported energy, 3 transportation, 4 products used by the organisation, 5 use of products from the organisation, and 6 other sources.

Category 1 maps to Scope 1 and category 2 to Scope 2. Categories 3 to 6 together are Scope 3, split on a different principle — ISO groups all transportation into one category where the GHG Protocol spreads it across four Scope 3 categories.
The totals reconcile exactly; the presentation does not. Reporting under both means presenting one inventory two ways, not computing it twice.

entries.title: Where ISO 14064-1 is stricter than the GHG Protocol
facts: ISO 14064-1:2018 requires an organisation to assess the significance of every indirect emission category and document its justification for anything excluded from the inventory.
That is a stronger obligation than the GHG Protocol's optional Scope 3. An inventory that satisfies the Corporate Standard by omitting Scope 3 does not satisfy ISO 14064-1.

Direct removals sit inside ISO category 1 alongside direct emissions, where the GHG Protocol handles removals separately — so a company with material removals shows a different category 1 than its Scope 1.

entries.title: ISO 14064-3 verification
facts: ISO 14064-3:2019 specifies requirements for validating and verifying GHG statements: selecting the verifier, agreeing the level of assurance, and setting objectives, criteria and scope.

Two levels: limited assurance gives a negative-form conclusion — nothing came to the verifier's attention suggesting material misstatement; reasonable assurance gives a positive-form conclusion after more extensive procedures.
Materiality is commonly set at 5% for reasonable assurance, and it drives the nature, timing and extent of the verification work.

The GHG Protocol has no verification standard of its own, so a GHG Protocol inventory is typically verified against ISO 14064-3 or ISAE 3410 — the accounting standard and the assurance standard are separate choices.
